description.narrative: Insatsen gäller stöd om 122 000 000 SEK till den andra fasen av Joint UN Programme on Social Protection under åren 2019 - 2024. Avtalspart är UNICEF och medverkande FN-organisationer är WFP, ILO och UNDP. Den första fasen genomfördes mellan 2016 och 2019 och fick stöd av Finland, Irland, UK samt Sverige. Fortsättningen bygger vidare på resultat och erfarenheter från den första fasen och har ett något snävare fokus på i första hand att bygga system och kapacitet kring socialbidragssystemet för de allra fattigaste i Zambia. Ytterligare viktiga komponenter är integrering av jämställdhet, anpassning för funktionshindrade, förbättrad nutrition för gravida och ammande kvinnor samt system för ökade utvecklingseffekter genom förbättrade länkar mellan socialbidrag och andra insatser sk Cash+. En ytterligare komponent gäller utbetalning av extra socialbidrag under 2019, 2020 och 2021 till mottagare i distrikt som är särskilt drabbade av torka och Covid 19. Programmets ska finansieras gemensamt av Sverige, UK och Schweiz.

Support to the second phase of the Joint UN Programme on Social Protection 2019-2024. Agreement partner is UNICEF and the participating UN Organisations are WFP and ILO. The first phase was implemented between 2016 and 2019 and was supported by Finland, Ireland, UK and Sweden. The continuation builds upon the results and lessons learned in the first phase but is more focused on building systems and capacity around the social cash transfers for the poorest in Zambia. Other important Components of the programme are mainstreaming of gender and disability, improved nutrition for pregnant and lactating mothers as well as increased development effects through enhanced operational links between social cash transfers and other initiatives, so called cash+. An additional component deals with Emergecy Cash Transfers during 2019, 2020 and 2021 to households that are hardest hit by the prolonged reduced rainfalls as well as Covid 19. The programme is to be funded by Sweden, UK and Switzerland.

The Joint UN Programme on Social Protection phase II has the following expected results:
Impact: Reduced Multi-dimentional poverty
Outcomes: 1. Predictable and regular Social Cash Transfers 2. Operational Cash linkages 3. Improved nutrition 4. Disability mainstreaming 5. Improved cluster perfomace In addition the programme has a component of Emergency Cash Transfers with payments during 2019 and 2020 to social cash beneficiaries in the districts hardest hit by the prolonged reduced rainfall.In 2020 another round of Emergency Cash Transfers has been added to mitigate the situation related to Covid-19. Sida plan to contribute financially to the covid-19 ECT through an amendment to the programme agreement.

description.narrative:
The programme has largely performed well during 2024, below some examples of results in summary:
Focus Area 1: Improved Regularity of the Social Cash Transfer (SCT): During the reporting period, the Social Cash Transfer (SCT) programme in Zambia achieved both anticipated and unforeseen outcomes. As expected, the programme expanded significantly in response to the 20232024 drought, reaching over 2.2 million householdswell above the annual target of 1.3 million. This included both vertical (increased transfer values) and horizontal (new beneficiaries) expansions, demonstrating the SCT systems enhanced shock responsiveness. The operationalisation of the SCT Performance Monitoring System and integration of ECTMIS improved programme oversight and data driven decision making. Evidence based analyses informed adjustments to transfer values and targeting strategies, particularly for vulnerable groups such as persons with disabilities and female headed households.
Unexpectedly, the programmes rapid scaleup capacity exceeded prior benchmarks, enrolling over 900,000 new households within two months. Additionally, the rollout of PSEA training across all 116 districts, including the training of 106 master trainers, marked a significant step in safeguarding beneficiaries. The integration of SCT households into the national health insurance scheme (NHIMA), covering over 112,000 individuals, also represented a notable advancement toward universal health coverage.
Advocacy efforts, including the launch of the Tisunge Zambia campaign, further elevated public awareness and policy engagement around social protection. These results collectively reflect a strengthened, more adaptive SCT system capable of addressing both chronic poverty and acute shocks.
Focus Area 2: Gender and nutrition sensitive social protection: The 1000 Days in SCT pilot achieved strong results, reaching over 12,900 households and integrating with the national drought response to support an additional 6,000. Expected outcomes included improved dietary diversity, food security, and access to services for nearly 37,000 children, supported by nutrition topups and community case management. Unexpectedly, the pilot also enabled 974 adolescent mothers to return to school and expanded access to reproductive health services for over 6,000 girls and women. The pilot is currently being scaled up to four new districts under the GEWEL programme, indicating well functioning working relationships between the UN and the World Bank.
Social accountability mechanisms, such as community scorecards and budget tracking tools, enhanced transparency and community engagement. Implementation research confirmed positive impacts but also highlighted gaps in structured needs assessments and the need for greater support and compensation for CWACs. The pilots integration of adolescent health, social protection, and communityled monitoring offers valuable lessons for future scaleup and systems strengthening.
Focus Area 3: Improved Disability Mainstreaming: 1. Harmonised Community Based Inclusive Development (CBID) guidelines and training manuals developed. 2. Rapid Assistive Technologies Assessment (RATA) done and Prioritised National Assistive Products List approved. 3. The National Disability Policy finalised with mainstreaming guidelines to operationalise its implementation. 4. Organisations for People with Disabilities (OPD) capacities on disability rights and inclusion enhanced.
Disability inclusion advanced through the development of harmonised CBID guidelines, a validated rightsbased assessment tool for children and adults, and the finalisation of the National Disability Policy. ZAPD launched its Strategic Plan and trained 26 disability focal points across ministries. Over 150 OPDs were trained in entrepreneurship, tripling the original target. 433 assistive devices were distributed using the new Assistive Products List. SCT access improved through staff training and integration of disability screening tools.
Focus Area 4: Improved performance of the poverty and vulnerability cluster: The National Social Protection Policy (NSPP) was approved, with its implementation and financing strategies under development. A national coordination strategy was also validated to improve inter ministerial collaboration. Institutional capacity was enhanced through the training of 13 national TRANSFORM master trainers and the development of a rollout plan. A draft Cash Plus Strategy was produced to link social cash transfers with complementary services in health, education, and livelihoods. The Single Window Initiative received technical support in 10 districts, with a review and staff training planned for 2025. Budget advocacy was reinforced through 22 budget briefs and technical inputs to the national budget, including a note on the impact of emergency transfers. Social accountability tools (manuals, budget tracking instruments, and scorecards) were developed to improve transparency and citizen engagement.
Challenges such as limited coordination, delayed legal reforms, and programme alignment issues were addressed through sustained advocacy, technical support, and stakeholder engagement.
Focus Area 5: Improved service delivery and interaction with beneficiaries and communities: In 2024, social accountability and community participation in social protection were strengthened through the development of 22 Ward Development Plans and the rollout of Community Balanced Scorecards in 22 districts. Over 500 district staff were trained in budget tracking, and civil society engagement increased via a new advocacy coalition and public awareness efforts. Community monitoring reached more than 680 participants, and new tools were introduced to improve transparency and feedback. In Katete, local input shaped the revised Integrated Development Plan. Programme visibility rose by 20% through coordinated media outreach. Several key studies were completed or launched, including evaluations of the 1000 Days pilot, urban SCT, and albinism rights, with further research on drought resilience, female headed households, and assistive technologies expected in 2025
